headline: Nandemo is, by surface analysis, 何で (“why, how”) plus も.
Oriru comes from a classical upper bigrade verb, 下る (oru).
Taezu is the negative continuative of 絶える (taeru, “to cease”).
Kawari, “substitute”, is the continuative stem of the verb 代わる (kawaru, “to substitute”).
Ito, “thread”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ito.
Tenisu kōto is simply English “tennis court”.
Mono, “person”, is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 and is cognate with 物 (mono, “thing”).
Nakunaru is literally “to become not”: the -ku form of 無い (nai, “not, missing”) plus なる (naru).
Fun'iki appeared in a physics book of 1827, translating Dutch lucht (“air”), before it came to mean “atmosphere”.
Shi, “death”, appears to be a conflation of Middle Chinese 死 with an Old Japanese root that sounded alike.
Shōgakukin is 奨学 (shōgaku) plus 金 (-kin).
Nochi is from Old Japanese, and its ultimate derivation is unknown.
Ka, “passable”, is from Middle Chinese 可.
Fujin, “madam”, is described as simply from Classical Chinese.
Gan, “cancer”, is from Middle Chinese 癌.
Iremono is the verb 入れる (ireru) plus 物 (-mono).
Hayaru is related to 早い (hayai, “early, fast”), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *paya.
Semaru, “to draw near”, is cognate with 攻める (semeru) and 狭い (semai).
Bangumi is 番 (ban, “turn”) plus 組み (kumi), with the k voiced to g by rendaku.
Aware originally meant “deeply touching or moving”, with no negative connotation.
Uraguchi is 裏 (ura, “back”) plus 口 (kuchi, “opening, door”), with kuchi voiced to guchi.
Aku, “evil”, is from Middle Chinese 惡.
Masukomi is short for masu komyunikēshon, “mass communication”.
Shō ga nai contracts 仕様がない (shiyō ga nai), literally “there is no way”.
Warau is derived from 割る (waru, “to split, to break”): “to be in the act of cracking up”.
Ijō is literally “deviance from normalcy”.
Chikyū is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 地球 (Dìqiú), coined by Matteo Ricci.
Shō as a suffix is a clipping of 小学校 (shōgakkō).
